title: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brings inoculation to England

confidence.note: Lady Mary's own letter and the surgeon Charles Maitland's 1722 account document the London inoculations of 1721. How much credit she deserves is a matter of emphasis: reports of the Ottoman practice reached the Royal Society before she did, and retellings differ on details such as the number of Newgate prisoners.

people: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu (1689–1762), writer and advocate of inoculation
Charles Maitland, Scottish embassy surgeon who performed the operations
Emanuel Timoni (1670–1718), physician in Constantinople who reported the practice to the Royal Society
summary: An ambassador's wife saw Ottoman women give children mild smallpox on purpose, tried it on her own son and daughter, and helped make it fashionable in London.
body: Writing from Adrianople (now Edirne) during her husband's posting as British ambassador to the Ottoman court, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu described what locals called "engrafting." Every autumn, old women opened a vein with a needle and put in a little matter from a mild case of smallpox; patients fell briefly ill and were then protected. She had survived smallpox herself, scarred, and had lost her brother to it, so she had her young son engrafted by an old Greek practitioner, assisted by the embassy surgeon Charles Maitland.

Back in London during the epidemic of 1721, she had Maitland inoculate her daughter in April before medical witnesses, the first such operation in Britain. That August, six condemned prisoners at Newgate were inoculated in return for pardons; five developed mild smallpox and the sixth turned out to have had it already. In 1722 two daughters of the Prince of Wales followed. Deaths after inoculation kept it controversial.

She was not the first to tell England about it: a physician in Constantinople, Emanuel Timoni, had described the practice in a letter read to the Royal Society in 1714. What Lady Mary supplied was proof on her own children and the social standing to make it respectable.

myth.tradition: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu discovered smallpox inoculation and single-handedly introduced it to Britain.
myth.record: Written accounts of the Ottoman practice had reached the Royal Society by 1714, and the operations in England were performed by the surgeon Charles Maitland. Her part was that of advocate, and of a parent who put her own children forward.

links.note: The same year, Boston learned inoculation from an enslaved West African man.
A different route to the same idea: smallpox scabs blown into the nose.
Jenner, inoculated as a child, replaced smallpox matter with cowpox.

title: Stephen Hales measures blood pressure

confidence.note: Hales dated the experiment only to "December"; his figures were already in print in *Vegetable Staticks* (1727) and the full description appeared in *Haemastaticks* (1733). The measurement itself is described in his own words and is not in doubt.

people: Stephen Hales (1677–1761), curate of Teddington and experimenter
summary: A country clergyman tied a horse down, ran a nine-foot glass tube into its artery, and watched the blood climb more than eight feet.
body: The earliest recorded measurement of blood pressure was made by a parish clergyman. Stephen Hales, curate of Teddington, tied a mare down on her back, opened the main artery of her thigh and joined it by brass pipes to a glass tube nine feet long. The blood rose 8 feet 3 inches above the level of her heart and rose and fell a few inches with each beat. He also measured dogs and a deer. The horses, already condemned as unfit for service, were bled out as he measured. Hales gave the figures briefly in 1727 and in full in *Haemastaticks* (1733).

links.note: Hales measured the force driving Harvey's circulation.

title: James Lind's scurvy trial

confidence.note: The only record of the trial is Lind's own four-page account, published six years later; one historian has suggested it may be fabricated because the men do not appear on the ship's sick list, but most accept it. What is firmly documented is how slowly and unevenly the Navy acted afterwards.

people: Gilbert Blane, physician and Sick and Hurt Board commissioner who won wider issue of lemon juice in 1795
summary: Twelve sick sailors, six remedies, two oranges and a lemon a day: an early fair test that worked, and a lesson the Navy took nearly fifty years to act on.
body: On 20 May 1747, aboard the warship *Salisbury* on blockade duty in the English Channel, the naval surgeon James Lind took twelve sailors sick with scurvy, men whose cases were, he wrote, "as similar as I could have them." They lay in the same quarters and ate the same basic diet. Lind gave two men each one of six remedies then in use: cider, elixir of vitriol (dilute sulfuric acid), vinegar, seawater, a paste of garlic, mustard seed and radish root, or two oranges and a lemon a day. The fruit ran out after six days, but by then one of the pair was fit for duty and the other was well enough to nurse the rest.

Twelve men is tiny, and Lind never said how he decided who got what. Still, his report is one of the earliest descriptions of a planned comparison that tried to hold everything else equal. It occupies about four pages of his 450-page *Treatise of the Scurvy* (1753), most of which is a critical review of everything written on the disease before him.

What Lind did next is the surprising part. He never stated plainly that citrus cured scurvy. He thought it a disease of faulty digestion and excretion, worsened by foul air, poor diet and lack of exercise, and he kept recommending other remedies. To make fruit portable he boiled juice down into a concentrate, a "rob," which later analysis showed held almost no vitamin C. The year after the *Treatise* appeared, the Navy's Sick and Hurt Board turned down a proposal to supply sailors with fruit juice.

Only in 1795 did the physician Gilbert Blane, by then a commissioner on that board, persuade the Admiralty to issue lemon juice on a large scale; by 1815 scurvy had almost vanished from the fleet. The heroic version, in which a lone genius is ignored by blockheads for forty years, was popularized in the 1890s. In fact the board was swamped with rival cures, and Lind never clearly urged lemon juice on it. Nor did the lesson stick: lime juice, which later replaced lemon, failed to keep scurvy off a British Arctic expedition in 1875–76.

myth.tradition: Lind proved that citrus cures scurvy, and the stubborn Admiralty ignored him for over forty years.
myth.record: Lind never clearly recommended lemon juice, pushed a heat-treated concentrate with little vitamin C, and blamed scurvy on several causes. The Navy's 1795 change followed Gilbert Blane's lobbying and further evidence gathered at sea.

links.note: Vitamin C explained, 160 years later, why the oranges worked.
Two centuries on, chance rather than the doctor decided who got what.
Another eighteenth-century step toward the fair test.

title: Morgagni: disease has a seat

confidence.note: The book and its date are not in question. Calling Morgagni the founder of pathological anatomy is the verdict of later historians; he built openly on an earlier collection of autopsy reports, and counts of his cases vary slightly (about 700).

people: Giovanni Battista Morgagni (1682–1771), professor of anatomy at Padua
summary: At seventy-nine, a Padua anatomist laid some 700 life stories beside their autopsies and showed that diseases live in particular organs.
body: In 1761, at the age of seventy-nine, the Padua anatomy professor Giovanni Battista Morgagni published *De sedibus et causis morborum per anatomen indagatis*, "on the seats and causes of diseases investigated by anatomy." Its five books hold seventy letters reporting about 700 cases. In each, he set what a patient had suffered in life beside what he, his teacher Valsalva or his friends found in the body after death, recording for his own cases the year, month and place.

The method was the message. If symptoms in life matched damage in a particular organ, then disease had a location, and the place to look for it was the organ rather than a whole-body imbalance of humors. Morgagni presented the work as material toward a better version of an older compilation of autopsy reports, the *Sepulchretum*. His book gave classic early descriptions of conditions including mitral stenosis, heart block and angina, and it was quickly translated into French (1765), English (1769) and German (1771).

links.note: Paris hospital doctors made bedside-to-autopsy correlation routine.
Laennec's stethoscope let doctors hear organ damage in the living.

title: John Hunter makes surgery a science

confidence.note: Hunter's career, publications and museum are well documented. The famous story that he inoculated himself with venereal matter rests on inference: his own account does not name the subject.

people: John Hunter (1728–1793), surgeon, anatomist and collector
summary: A Scottish farm boy who quit school at 13 became London's leading surgeon by testing operations on animals first and dissecting the results.
body: John Hunter came to London from a Scottish farm in 1748 to help in his brother William's anatomy school, and by the late 1780s he was widely seen as the leading surgeon of his day. His creed was observation and experiment. In 1785 he treated a coachman's popliteal aneurysm by tying off the artery higher in the thigh, an idea he had first tested on animals, and later obtained the leg to see the result. His museum held nearly 14,000 specimens at his death in 1793.

myth.tradition: Hunter heroically inoculated himself with gonorrhea and gave himself syphilis.
myth.record: Hunter described inoculating an unnamed subject. His biographer Wendy Moore thinks it was almost certainly him, but it cannot be proven, and the contaminated matter led him to the wrong conclusion that the two diseases were one.

links.note: Hunter relied on body-snatchers all his life.

title: Mesmerism on trial

confidence.note: The commission, its experiments and its report of 1784 are fully documented. Who designed the blind tests is not: the report credits no individual, and the case for Lavoisier rests on his private papers and a single letter.

people: Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815), physician and promoter of animal magnetism
Charles Deslon, Mesmer's former associate, who demonstrated the method
summary: To test a fashionable cure, a royal commission blindfolded the patients, and invented one of the most powerful tools in medicine.
body: Franz Anton Mesmer, an Austrian physician, came to Paris after a scandal in Vienna in 1777, claiming that an invisible fluid, "animal magnetism," filled the universe and that illness came from obstacles to its flow. His practitioners provoked dramatic "crises" in patients. In 1784 Louis XVI appointed a royal commission of nine, including Benjamin Franklin and the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, to examine the method as practiced by Mesmer's former associate Charles Deslon. Mesmer refused to let anyone test whether the fluid existed.

The commissioners set out to separate the fluid from what they called "the imagination." At Franklin's house in Passy and elsewhere, blindfolded subjects who were told they were being magnetized when nobody was doing it fell into crisis anyway. The commission concluded that the effects came from no physical force, and that the treatment was ineffective and undesirable. These are the first known experiments to use blind comparisons to judge a treatment.
Mesmerism lost its standing in French medicine, though related methods based on suggestion, including hypnosis, lived on.

myth.tradition: Benjamin Franklin devised the blind tests that debunked Mesmer.
myth.record: The report credits no individual. Lavoisier's papers contain a plan of experiments in his own hand, and a letter from the commission's chairman, Bailly, suggests Franklin was only told of the plan on the day, so Lavoisier is the likelier designer.

links.note: Another eighteenth-century step toward the fair test.
Placebo-controlled tests were later turned on homeopathy.
Blinding became a pillar of the modern controlled trial.

title: Withering and the foxglove

confidence.note: The book and its 163 cases are documented. The story of how Withering came to the plant rests on his own brief account, and he was not alone: colleagues were already using foxglove.

summary: A Birmingham doctor picked foxglove out of a twenty-herb folk remedy and reported every case, failures included.
body: In 1775 the physician William Withering, newly arrived in Birmingham, was asked about a family recipe for dropsy that an old woman in Shropshire had long kept secret. It contained twenty or more herbs, and he judged that the active one must be foxglove. Over the next decade he learned to dry and dose the leaf, and in *An Account of the Foxglove* (1785) he reported 163 patients, successes and failures alike, refusing to publish only flattering cases. He described its side effects, including nausea and yellow-green vision.

myth.tradition: A Shropshire herbalist called Mother Hutton gave Withering the foxglove cure.
myth.record: Withering never named her: his 1785 book mentions only an anonymous old woman in Shropshire, and the name Mother Hutton does not appear in it. Colleagues such as John Ash were also already using the plant.

links.note: Another early attempt to judge a remedy honestly.
